title: How the heart moves blood — and keeps two circuits apart

standards.text: Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms.
standards.howThisLessonMeetsIt: The student manipulates a system model: they explode it to expose components, trace matter flow through it, then rebuild it from parts and name each component's function.

standards.text: Use argument supported by evidence for how the body is a system of interacting subsystems composed of groups of cells.
standards.practice: SEP-7 Engaging in Argument from Evidence
standards.note: Circulatory system is inside this expectation's assessment boundary.

bigQuestion.hs: Blood returns from your body and leaves for your lungs many times a minute. How does the heart move both supplies without letting them mix?
bigQuestion.ms: Blood comes back from your body and then goes to your lungs to pick up oxygen. How does the heart pump both trips without mixing them?

text.hs: Name the four chambers and the four valves, and say which side of the heart each belongs to.
text.ms: Name the four chambers and the two big valves on each side.

text.hs: Put the parts in the exact order blood passes through them, from the venae cavae to the aorta.
text.ms: Put the parts in the order blood flows through the heart.

text.hs: Explain how wall thickness and valve parts show structure–function fit.
text.ms: Say why one pumping chamber has a thicker wall.

text.hs: Reject the rule 'arteries carry oxygen-rich blood' by naming the exception.
text.ms: Explain that the vessel going to the lungs carries blood low in oxygen.

tiers.why: Core tier = the 4 chambers and 4 valves: 41–144 mm across, comfortable to point at with a controller ray. Detail tier = septum plus 5 papillary muscles; two of them measure only 12 mm, so naming them cold in VR is frustrating rather than informative. Detail tier is optional and uses enlarged hit spheres.

flow.note: Ordered path students must reconstruct. Chambers and valves are real registry parts; the four 'waypoint' entries are schematic text+arrow markers generated by the app, because this GLB contains no great vessels. Waypoints are anchored to a real part and offset in model metres (model frame: +y superior, +x patient-left, +z anterior).

steps.title: Meet the heart in place

prompt.hs: This is the heart sitting in the chest. Before anything moves: which side do you think holds the blood that has already given up its oxygen?
prompt.ms: Look at the heart. Which half do you think holds blood that has already dropped off its oxygen?

steps.why: Committing to a prediction before the model is taken apart makes the later explanation something the student needs, not something they receive.

steps.title: Pull it apart

prompt.hs: Slowly explode the model. Say out loud what separates from what, and which pieces were hidden inside. Then name the four chambers you can now see from every angle.
prompt.ms: Slowly pull the heart apart. Say what comes out. Point at the four rooms.

steps.why: Exploding is the model-building move HS-LS1-2 asks for; narrating while doing it is self-explanation, which is what makes the manipulation stick.

steps.title: Two pumps, not one

prompt.hs: Isolate the left ventricle, then the right. Compare their wall thickness. Why would the body's supply need a thicker wall than the lungs' supply?
prompt.ms: Look at the big pumping room on each side. One wall is thicker. Why would that one need to push harder?

steps.why: Structure–function reasoning is the transferable idea; the wall-thickness contrast is the visible evidence for it.

steps.title: Follow one drop of blood

prompt.hs: Click the parts in the order one drop of blood passes through them, starting where blood enters from the body.
prompt.ms: Click the parts in the order blood flows through the heart.

steps.why: Ordering the components is the systems-model claim itself, and it is the first retrieval practice in the lesson.

steps.title: Put it back and name it

prompt.hs: Assemble the heart, then name every part you are asked to find — no labels this time.
prompt.ms: Put the heart back together, then point at each part you are asked for.

steps.why: Cold naming after labels are removed is retrieval practice; it is the part that produces durable memory, and it is also the formative check the student sees instantly.

def.hs: A receiving chamber that fills from a vein and pumps into the ventricle below it.
def.ms: An upper room that lets blood in.

def.hs: A pumping chamber that pushes blood out through a semilunar valve into a vessel.
def.ms: A lower room that pushes blood out.

def.hs: A flap that opens one way and stops blood flowing backwards.
def.ms: A door that only opens one way.

def.hs: The wall between the two halves; it is what keeps the two circuits from mixing.
def.ms: The wall down the middle that keeps the two sides apart.

def.hs: The heart's own muscle layer; its thickness shows how hard a chamber pushes.
def.ms: The muscle of the heart wall.

correction.hs: A vessel is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, not because of how much oxygen it holds. The pulmonary trunk carries blood low in oxygen from the right ventricle to the lungs.
correction.ms: The tube going to the lungs carries blood that is low in oxygen, even though it leaves the heart.

misconceptions.surfacedAs: The 'to the lungs' waypoint is a vessel leaving the heart that carries blood low in oxygen — the moment the rule breaks.
misconceptions.source: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

misconceptions.claim: The heart pumps blood from the lungs and the body into one shared chamber.

correction.hs: The septum separates the two halves, so right-side and left-side blood never share a chamber; the two circuits are in series, not pooled.
correction.ms: The wall down the middle keeps the two trips of blood apart.

misconceptions.surfacedAs: Exploding exposes the interventricular septum as a separate part, which is the physical reason the two circuits stay apart.
misconceptions.source: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, 19.1 Heart Anatomy

quiz.q: Which valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle?
quiz.why: The mitral (bicuspid) valve guards the left atrium-to-ventricle opening; the tricuspid guards the right side.
quiz.source: adapted from OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 19 review question

quiz.q: Which lists the valves in the order blood passes through them, from the vena cava onward?
quiz.why: Right side first (tricuspid then pulmonary), through the lungs, then left side (mitral then aortic).
quiz.source: adapted from OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 19 review question

quiz.q: Which chamber first receives blood returning from the body?
quiz.why: The venae cavae empty into the right atrium.
quiz.source: adapted from OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 19 review question

quiz.q: In which chamber would you find the thickest myocardium?
quiz.why: The left ventricle drives the systemic circuit, at much higher pressure than the pulmonary circuit.
quiz.source: adapted from OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 19 review question

runtime.note: Tunable by a teacher without touching code. Explode gain was measured in a browser run: gain 0.55 gave 14/14 draw calls with a 0.96 m exploded extent; gain 1.0 pushed parts out of the camera frustum (draw calls fell 14 -> 11).

ui.note: AUTHORED IN DEGREES OF VIEW, NOT METRES. Quest 2 puts ~18.5 px on every degree (1832 px per eye across ~99 deg); a desktop preview has FEWER px per degree, so judge legibility by angle, never by screenshot pixels. Position is COMPUTED, not hand-placed: the runtime measures the exploded cloud's real angular width from the student's eye and puts the card outside it with panelGapDeg of clearance. Hand-placing the card in metres is what kept putting it on the organ - a 0.28 m card at 0.34 m covers ~44 deg of view while the exploded cloud is ~32 deg wide, so even '0.16 m to the left' overlapped ~14% of it. Text in degrees converts to a fixed pixel height on the lens regardless of model scale: 1.45 deg = ~27 px.
